input:
## Case
This proposal sets out the case for a rooftop solar installation, and explains why approval is being sought to take the project forward to the detailed design stage. The underlying idea is a straightforward and appealing one. The site in question has a large roof that is not currently used for any productive purpose, and the site also consumes electricity in the course of its normal operations. By placing solar generation on the roof, the site would be able to generate power on its own premises, at the point where that power is used, and on a surface that already exists and is currently doing nothing.

It is important to be clear, at the same time, about what stage the project has reached and what it has not. A number of the figures that would be needed to make a complete financial case for the installation are not yet available. Nobody has yet established exactly how much power an array on this roof would generate over the course of a year, what proportion of that output the site would be able to use itself, or on what terms any surplus might be exported. All of these are, in the nature of things, outputs of a design exercise, and until that exercise has been carried out, they can only be guessed at. For that reason, this proposal does not attempt to claim that the installation will definitely pay for itself, or to put a figure on the benefit it will deliver. What it does claim is that the combination of circumstances at the site — a large unused roof, and a demand for electricity on the same premises — makes the idea well worth taking to the next stage, and that the open questions are precisely the kind of questions that a detailed design is intended to answer.

## Costs
The capital cost of the installation is estimated at $1236k. The appraisal of the project is carried out over a horizon of 7 years.

The figure of $1236k is intended to represent the whole of the capital commitment: the solar array itself and the mounting system that holds it on the roof, the inverters and electrical connection equipment, the cabling and protection, and the installation and commissioning work required to bring the complete system into service. It is a single, all-in figure, and the appraisal is conducted on the basis of that figure rather than on a series of separate allowances that might later be added together. No savings have been netted off against it, and nothing has been held back.

Other elements of the financial picture are, for the reasons given above, not yet stated. The running costs of the installation, the value of the electricity it will generate, and the arrangements for exporting any surplus all depend on decisions and calculations that belong to the design stage: the layout that the design finally settles on, the yield that it calculates, and the connection that it agrees. Once those are known, a proper appraisal over the 7 years of the appraisal horizon can be put together; until then, any appraisal would rest on assumptions that this proposal is not in a position to support.

## Schedule
It is proposed that work would start one quarter after approval is given.

The work would proceed in a logical sequence. The first stage is detailed design, which covers the layout of the array, the checking of the roof structure, the electrical design, and the application for connection, and it is only when the design has been fixed that it makes sense to buy anything. Procurement follows, against the specification that the design produces. Installation comes after procurement, and connection and commissioning bring the sequence to a close. It should be noted that no contractor is named anywhere in this proposal. This is deliberate: the appointment of a contractor belongs to the procurement stage, and it ought to be made on the basis of the finished design rather than in advance of it.

The schedule is expressed in terms of a starting point and an order of stages, rather than as a programme of fixed dates. The dates of the later stages will depend to a considerable extent on what the design finds, and on the connection process, and neither of these can be pinned down in advance. What can be stated firmly is the order in which things will happen, and the point from which they will start to happen, namely one quarter after approval.

## Decision requested
The decision that is being requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. Nothing more than that is being asked for. In particular, this proposal does not request approval to construct the installation, and approving this proposal should not be taken as approving construction.

The detailed design will produce the information that a construction decision requires: a fixed layout, a calculated yield, the capital cost confirmed against the figure of $1236k quoted at this stage, and the terms on which connection will be granted. When that information is available, the case for or against construction can be made properly, on real figures instead of on the general fit between a roof and a demand for power, and it will be made in a separate proposal.

The commitment involved in approving this proposal is accordingly a limited one: it is the cost and the time of the design stage itself. If the design were to show that the roof could not carry the installation, or that the yield did not justify the capital cost, or that the connection terms were unacceptable, then the project could simply be stopped at that point, and the construction question would never have to be put at all. If, on the other hand, the design supports the case, the decision that follows will be a decision about a fully designed installation with a confirmed price attached to it. Either way, the decision being requested at this stage is the smaller and better-informed one, and it is the decision that the current state of the information supports.
target:
## Case
Approval is sought to take a rooftop solar installation to detailed design. The case is for the design stage, and it is made on the site's position rather than on a finished yield figure.

The site buys the electricity it uses, and its roof is a large surface that currently does no work. A rooftop installation puts generation on that surface, at the point where the power is consumed, without taking land or building volume from the operation the site exists for. The fit between the asset and the use is the substance of the case: the generation and the demand stand in the same place, under the same ownership, and the installation asks nothing of the site except the roof it already has.

What the case does not yet rest on is a settled account of value. The yield of the array, the share of the output the site would consume, and the terms on which any surplus would leave the site are all quantities that a design fixes, and none of them is stated here as a fact. The proposal therefore does not argue that the installation pays, because the figures that would carry that argument are not yet in hand. It argues the narrower point: that the site's position makes the installation worth designing, that the questions standing between the concept and a construction decision are design questions, and that they can only be answered by doing the design. The case is for finding out, made because the finding-out is small against the commitment it would inform, and because the site's circumstances give the answer a real chance of being favourable.

## Costs
The capital cost of the installation is $1236k. The appraisal horizon is 7 years.

The capital figure is the installed cost of the complete system: the array and its mounting, the inversion and connection equipment, the cabling and protection, and the installation work that puts them in place and brings the system into service. It is a single figure for the whole commitment, and it is the figure the appraisal runs on. No part of it is held back as a later addition, and no saving is netted against it at this stage.

Running costs, the value of the generated power, and the terms for any export are not stated in this proposal, because each of them depends on the design: on the layout the design settles, the yield it calculates, and the connection it agrees. An appraisal over the 7-year horizon can be assembled once the design returns those quantities, and it cannot be assembled honestly before. The costs section therefore fixes what is known, the capital commitment of $1236k and the horizon over which it is judged, and leaves the rest of the account open, marked as design output rather than filled with estimates.

## Schedule
Work starts one quarter after approval.

The sequence runs in the order the work requires. Detailed design comes first: the layout, the structural check of the roof, the electrical design, and the connection application all belong to it, and nothing is procured against a design that has not been fixed. Procurement follows the design, on the design's specification. Installation follows procurement, and connection and commissioning close the sequence. No contractor is named in this proposal, because the appointment belongs to the procurement stage and is made against the finished design.

The schedule is stated as a sequence and a start, not as a dated programme. Dates for the later stages depend on the design's findings and on the connection process, neither of which this proposal can settle in advance. What is fixed is the order, and the point from which the order runs: one quarter after approval, the design stage opens.

## Decision requested
The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. Construction is not requested, and approval of this proposal does not approve it.

Detailed design returns the quantities the construction decision needs: a fixed layout, a calculated yield, the confirmed capital cost against the $1236k now stated, and the connection terms. With those in hand, the construction case can be made on figures rather than on the fit between a roof and a site's demand, and it will be made as a separate proposal to the same decision body.

The exposure accepted by approving this proposal is the design stage itself. If the design shows that the roof will not carry the array, that the yield does not support the capital cost, or that the connection terms fail the appraisal, the project stops at the design, and the construction question is never put. If the design sustains the case, the decision that follows is a decision on a designed installation at a confirmed cost. Either way, the decision requested now is the smaller one, and it is the one the present state of the figures supports.
